questions.prompt: On a quadratic, the conjugate-gradient direction is
options: the Newton step, requiring the Hessian to be factored
a fixed vector chosen before the first gradient is evaluated
the negative gradient on the first iteration, and thereafter the negative gradient plus a multiple of the previous direction
always the negative gradient, with the multiple forced to zero
questions.explanation: The first direction has no previous direction to add, so it is the negative gradient. Each later direction is \(-\nabla f + \beta d_{\mathrm{prev}}\), and \(\beta\) is chosen so the new direction is \(Q\)-conjugate to the previous one. Forcing \(\beta = 0\) forever is steepest descent. The Newton step solves a linear system with the Hessian. The direction is recomputed from the gradient. It is not frozen in advance.

questions.prompt: The previous gradient is \((3,\ 0)\) and the new gradient is \((0,\ 2)\). The squared-norm formula gives \(\beta\) as the new squared length divided by the old squared length. What is \(\beta\)?
questions.explanation: The new squared length is \(0 + 4 = 4\). The old squared length is \(9 + 0 = 9\). The ratio is \(4/9\). Reporting \(9/4\) inverts the ratio. Reporting \(2/3\) divides the lengths instead of the squared lengths. Reporting \(4\) forgets the division by \(9\). The two gradients are orthogonal, which is what this iteration produces, and that fact is not itself the value of \(\beta\).

questions.prompt: In exact arithmetic, conjugate gradient on a positive definite quadratic of dimension \(n\)
options: can require more than \(n\) iterations even when every product is exact
reaches the minimizer in at most \(n\) iterations, with one multiplication by \(Q\) per iteration
reaches the minimizer in one iteration, for every \(n\)
needs a matrix factorization whose cost grows like \(n^3\) at every iteration
questions.explanation: Each iteration adds one new conjugate direction, and \(n\) conjugate directions with exact line search finish the quadratic. The work in an iteration is the product of \(Q\) with a vector, plus a few vector updates. One iteration finishes only the one-dimensional case. A factorization is what this recursion avoids. Past \(n\) steps there is no new conjugate direction left. In exact arithmetic the gradient is already zero.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of one later conjugate-gradient iteration in order. Each step uses the result of the step before it.
questions.explanation: The quotient uses the new gradient, so the gradient comes first. The direction update uses that quotient, so it comes after the division. The line search walks along the direction just built, so the point cannot move before the direction exists. There is no branch in this later iteration: the previous direction is already there, and the first-iteration shortcut that skips \(\beta\) is a different iteration.

steps: Evaluate the gradient at the new point.
Divide the squared length of that new gradient by the squared length of the previous gradient. Call the quotient \(\beta\).
Using that \(\beta\), add \(\beta\) times the previous direction to the negative of the new gradient.
Using that new direction, take the exact line-search step and replace the current point.

questions.prompt: Which claims about conjugate gradient on a positive definite quadratic are true?
options: The first direction equals the negative gradient.
Each later multiple is chosen so the new direction is \(Q\)-conjugate to the previous direction.
Every iteration factors the Hessian.
Exact arithmetic reaches the minimizer in at most \(n\) steps in dimension \(n\).
The multiple is zero at every iteration, so every direction is the negative gradient.
questions.explanation:
The first direction has nothing to combine with, so it is \(-\nabla f\).
• The later update is \(-\nabla f + \beta d\), and \(\beta\) is the value that makes the \(Q\)-product with the previous direction vanish.
• A factorization is not part of the iteration. The product with \(Q\) is.
• At most \(n\) conjugate directions exist in an \(n\)-dimensional space, and exact search along all of them finishes a positive definite quadratic.
• A zero multiple at every iteration would be steepest descent. The multiple is zero on the first iteration and is not required to stay zero.

questions.prompt: The Hessian is diagonal with positive entries \(a\) and \(b\). The gradient is \((p,\ q)\), and the first direction is the negative gradient. The exact step length along that direction equals
questions.explanation: The direction is \((-p,\ -q)\). The numerator of the exact length is the negative of the directional derivative, which equals \(p^2 + q^2\). The curvature is \(a p^2 + b q^2\). Every declared name appears. The reciprocal \((a p^2 + b q^2)/(p^2 + q^2)\) inverts the length. Dropping \(a\) and \(b\), which leaves \(1\), treats the Hessian as the identity. Using \(p + q\) in place of the squared length drops the squares.

questions.prompt: A note builds the next conjugate-gradient direction from gradients \((0,\ 6)\) and \((3,\ 0)\), whose previous direction was the negative of \((3,\ 0)\). Exactly one step is a false claim.
questions.explanation: The gradients and the squared lengths are as stated, and \(36/9 = 4\). The direction update adds \(\beta\) times the previous direction, not \(\beta\) times the previous gradient. The previous direction is \((-3,\ 0)\). The next direction is \((0,\ -6) + 4\cdot(-3,\ 0) = (-12,\ -6)\). The displayed vector \((12,\ -6)\) is what the opposite sign in that slot produces. The arithmetic of \(-(0,\ 6) + 4\cdot(3,\ 0)\) really is \((12,\ -6)\). That vector is just not the direction.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 280 210" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>two arrows from the origin</title><line x1="46" y1="161.7" x2="250" y2="161.7"/><polygon points="250,161.7 243.6,164.4 243.6,159" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="60.1" y1="176" x2="60.1" y2="28"/><polygon points="60.1,28 62.8,34.4 57.3,34.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="248" y="175.7" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="66.1" y="30" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><line x1="60.1" y1="161.7" x2="235.9" y2="138.9"/><polygon points="235.9,138.9 229.9,142.5 229.2,137.1" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="243.9" y="130.9" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">u</text><line x1="60.1" y1="161.7" x2="118.7" y2="42.3"/><polygon points="118.7,42.3 118.3,49.3 113.4,46.9" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="126.7" y="34.3" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">v</text></svg>
steps: The new gradient is \((0,\ 6)\) and the old gradient is \((3,\ 0)\).
reasons: The update adds \(\beta\) times the previous direction. That direction is \((-3,\ 0)\), so the result is \((-12,\ -6)\), not \((12,\ -6)\).
The squared length of \((0,\ 6)\) is not \(36\).

questions.prompt: The gradient is \((4,\ 2)\) and \(Q = \mathrm{diag}(1,\ 2)\). The first direction is the negative gradient. What is the exact step length?
questions.explanation: The squared gradient length is \(16 + 4 = 20\). The curvature of the negative gradient equals the curvature of the gradient, \( (4,\ 2)\cdot(4,\ 4) = 16 + 8 = 24 \). The length is \(20/24 = 5/6\). Reporting \(24/20\) inverts the quotient. Reporting \(20\) drops the curvature. Reporting \(1\) would be the length if \(Q\) were the identity and the same cancellation happened, which it does not: the second diagonal entry is \(2\), and that is why the curvature is \(24\) rather than \(20\).
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping downward on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: The standard conjugate-gradient bound, for condition number \(\kappa\), says that the \(Q\)-norm of the error after \(k\) steps is at most
options: \(2\big((\sqrt{\kappa}-1)/(\sqrt{\kappa}+1)\big)^k\) times the initial \(Q\)-norm error
\(((\kappa-1)/(\kappa+1))^2\) times the previous function gap, which is the steepest-descent guarantee
a constant times the square of the previous error, from any start
\(1/k\), as a bound on the distance to the minimizer for every smooth convex function
questions.explanation: The conjugate-gradient factor uses the square root of \(\kappa\), and the quantity it multiplies is the \(Q\)-norm of the error. The leading \(2\) is part of that bound. The unsquared-root factor \(((\kappa-1)/(\kappa+1))^2\) is the steepest-descent bound on the function gap, a different claim. A constant times the squared error is the local Newton claim. A reciprocal of \(k\) is a sublinear pattern and is not this bound.
questions.figure_alt: A curve that falls toward the horizontal axis.

questions.prompt: The same direction update, used on a smooth objective that is not quadratic, is nonlinear conjugate gradient. What is lost?
options: The ability to evaluate a gradient.
Every use of the previous direction, so the update collapses to the Newton step.
The step length, which must then be exactly \(1\).
Finite termination in at most \(n\) steps. The conjugacy that proved it used a constant Hessian.
questions.explanation: The finite-termination argument expands the error in directions that are conjugate with respect to one fixed positive definite Hessian. A nonquadratic objective has a changing Hessian, so that expansion does not close after \(n\) steps. The gradient is still what the update uses. The previous direction is still added. The step length is still chosen by a line search. It is not frozen at \(1\). Restarts are a practical response to the lost termination, not a proof that termination remains.
questions.figure_alt: A curve that drops at first and then flattens.

questions.prompt: For condition number \(\kappa = 4\), the base \((\sqrt{\kappa}-1)/(\sqrt{\kappa}+1)\) in the conjugate-gradient error bound equals
questions.explanation: \(\sqrt{4} = 2\), so the base is \((2-1)/(2+1) = 1/3\). Reporting \((4-1)/(4+1) = 4/5\) uses \(\kappa\) without the square root. That is the steepest-descent shape, not this one. Reporting \(1/9\) squares the base, which is the heavy-ball momentum coefficient for this condition number, not the conjugate-gradient base. Reporting \(2\) is \(\sqrt{\kappa}\). The leading \(2\) in the full bound is a multiplier in front of the power of this base. It is not the base.
questions.figure_alt: A curve that falls toward the horizontal axis.

questions.prompt: A momentum method that adds a fraction of the previous displacement, instead of building a \(Q\)-conjugate direction, is
options: a Newton step, which solves the Hessian against the gradient
an exact line search that is required to stop at a conjugate direction
the heavy-ball update, which reads the gradient at the current point
a simplex pivot, which swaps one basic column
questions.explanation: Heavy ball steps from the current point along the negative gradient and then adds a multiple of the previous displacement. It does not enforce \(d^T Q d_{\mathrm{prev}} = 0\). A simplex pivot changes a basis of a linear program. Newton uses the Hessian as a linear operator. Exact line search chooses a length along a direction that already exists. It does not by itself create conjugacy.
